AND THE BRACKET THIS CARD ONCE HAD IS WITHDRAWN, NOT LOST: its at-or-before leg was tax_1833 alone. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Morrison, Orsemus” (tax_1833_076, line 128). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. merge_ruling.for_merge: The surname agrees letter for letter, d and s are one substitution apart in a worn impression, and Orsemus Morrison is one of the town's documented carpenters: the 1833 tax list, Fergus 1843 ('Morrison, Orsemus, carpenter, res 153 Clark [died Jan. 4,1864, a. 58½]') and Norris 1844 ('carpenter, house Clark st'). 'Ordemus' is a forename that exists nowhere else in the corpus, which is the profile of a mis-read rather than a man.
merge_ruling.against_merge: TWO ROLLS OF ONE TRANSCRIPTION, AND NEITHER SETS BOTH. 'Morrison, Orsemus' is the 1833 tax list (line 128) and 'Morrison, Ordemus' the poll filed 11 August 1834 (line 245) — and that poll also enters 'Morrison, J. M.' at line 244, so the roll that set Ordemus was setting Morrisons carefully. No roll sets both forenames; a shared source id is not a shared printing. The town holds five Morrison cards, so the surname decides nothing. D9, and the forename's absence from the rest of the corpus is kept in `for_merge` because it is what a reading of the 1834 poll's image would test.
